question: What are the stages of the classic SCOR model?
reference: Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return (plus Enable).
retrieved_contexts:
---
type: concept
title: SCOR model and core supply chain terms
description: Plan-Source-Make-Deliver-Return framing and the vocabulary interviewers expect
---
The classic SCOR model splits the chain into Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return (plus Enable). The newer SCOR Digital Standard renamed some of these; verify the current labels if you cite it by name.

Useful terms: FTL vs LTL, cross-dock (no storage, direct transfer), 3PL, inbound vs outbound logistics, MTS / MTO / ATO / ETO (make-to-stock, make-to-order, assemble-to-order, engineer-to-order), push vs pull, and the customer order decoupling point (where forecast-driven push turns into order-driven pull).

Interviewers use this to check you speak the planner's language. Tie every model you mention to a metric, see [supply chain metrics](supply-chain-metrics.md). Decisions by function are in the [planning hierarchy](planning-hierarchy.md).

question: How is OTIF calculated?
reference: Orders delivered on time and in full divided by total orders.
retrieved_contexts:
---
type: metric
title: Key supply chain metrics
description: Fill rate, OTIF, perfect order, inventory turns, days of supply, cash-to-cash, forecast accuracy, OEE, cost to serve
---
| Metric | Formula | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Unit fill rate | Units shipped from stock on first attempt / units ordered | Line fill and order fill are stricter variants |
| OTIF | Orders delivered on time and in full / total orders | Definition of "on time" (requested vs promised date) varies by client |
| Perfect order rate | Share of orders that are OTIF, undamaged and correctly documented | Often approximated as a product of component rates (assumes independence) |
| Inventory turns | COGS / average inventory value | Higher is leaner, but too high risks stockouts |
| Days of supply (DOS / DOH) | Average inventory / average daily COGS, or 365 / turns | Forward-looking DOS uses forecast demand instead |
| Cash-to-cash cycle | DIO + DSO - DPO | Inventory (DIO) is the lever SC teams own |
| Forecast accuracy | 1 - WMAPE | Measure at the grain and lag that drives decisions; see [forecast accuracy metrics](forecast-accuracy-metrics.md) |
| Forecast bias | Sum(F - A) / Sum(A) | Persistent positive bias = excess stock |
| OEE | Availability x Performance x Quality | Manufacturing only |
| Cost to serve | Total cost (logistics, handling, service) per customer or order | Reveals unprofitable customers/channels |

Self-test: fill rate 92% but OTIF 70%? Fill rate counts units; OTIF fails the whole order if any line is short or late. Many orders are missing a few lines, or are complete but late. Check lateness separately.

question: What are the four causes of the bullwhip effect?
reference: Demand signal processing, order batching, price fluctuations (promotions and forward buying), and rationing and shortage gaming.
retrieved_contexts:
---
type: concept
title: Bullwhip effect
description: Order variability amplifying upstream, its four causes and remedies
---
Order variability amplifies as you move upstream from retailer to supplier. Measured as Var(orders) / Var(demand) > 1 at each stage.

Four causes (Lee, Padmanabhan and Whang, 1997):
1. Demand signal processing: each stage forecasts from the orders it receives, not true demand.
2. Order batching: periodic or full-truckload ordering creates lumpy orders.
3. Price fluctuations: promotions and forward buying.
4. Rationing and shortage gaming: customers inflate orders when supply is short.

Remedies: share POS data, VMI, CPFR, smaller and more frequent orders, everyday low pricing, allocate shortages on past sales rather than current orders.

Cost to a client and how to show it: plot order variance vs POS demand variance by tier; the excess drives capacity, overtime and safety stock upstream (see [safety stock](safety-stock-and-rop.md)).
response:
The four causes of the bullwhip effect are:
1. Demand signal processing
2. Order batching
3. Price fluctuations
4. Rationing and shortage gaming

question: What is the EOQ formula?
reference: Q* = sqrt(2DS / h), where D is annual demand, S is the cost per order and h is the annual holding cost per unit.
retrieved_contexts:
---
type: formula
title: Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)
description: EOQ formula, robustness, worked example, EPQ and quantity discounts
---
Assumes constant known demand, fixed lead time, no shortages, instant replenishment.

TC(Q) = (D/Q) S + (Q/2) h, and Q* = sqrt(2DS / h). At Q*, annual ordering cost = annual holding cost.

Robustness: TC(Q)/TC(Q*) = 1/2 (Q/Q* + Q*/Q). Ordering 20% above Q* raises cost only about 1.7%; ordering 2x Q* raises it 25%. This flatness is why EOQ works despite rough cost inputs.

Worked example: D = 12,000 units/yr, S = Rs 500/order, c = Rs 200, i = 25%, so h = Rs 50. Q* = sqrt(2 x 12,000 x 500 / 50) is about 490 units, about 24.5 orders a year, total cost about Rs 24,500.

Extensions:
- EPQ (production rate P > demand rate D): Q* = sqrt(2DS / (h(1 - D/P))).
- Quantity discounts: compute Q* at each price; if it falls below that price's break, push it up to the break; pick the lowest total cost including purchase cost.

Cost parameters are explained in [why inventory exists](inventory-types.md).
response: TC(Q) = (D/Q) S + (Q/2) h, and Q* = sqrt(2DS / h).

question: What z-value corresponds to a 95% cycle service level?
retrieved_contexts:
---
type: formula
title: Safety stock and reorder point
description: SS formulas with demand and lead-time variability, z-values, worked example and refinements
---
SS = z x sigma_d x sqrt(L) (demand variability only).
SS = z x sqrt(L x sigma_d^2 + d-bar^2 x sigma_L^2) (demand and lead-time variability).
ROP = d-bar x L + SS.

z from target cycle service level: 90% -> 1.28, 95% -> 1.645, 98% -> 2.05, 99% -> 2.33.

Worked example: d-bar = 100/day, sigma_d = 20, L = 9 days, 95% CSL.
- Demand variability only: SS = 1.645 x 20 x 3 = about 99, ROP = 900 + 99 = 999.
- Add lead-time sigma_L = 2 days: SS = 1.645 x sqrt(9 x 400 + 10,000 x 4) = 1.645 x sqrt(43,600) = about 344.

Insight to say out loud: lead-time variability more than tripled safety stock. Fixing supplier reliability can free more cash than better forecasting. Lead-time variance enters multiplied by d-bar^2, so it often dominates.

Two refinements interviewers like:
1. sigma_d should be the forecast error standard deviation, not raw demand sigma. Seasonal demand has high sigma but may be well forecast. Safety stock covers what you can't predict. Better forecasts translate directly into lower stock (see [forecast accuracy metrics](forecast-accuracy-metrics.md)); quantify that for the client in rupees, not WMAPE points.
2. The formula targets CSL. For a fill rate target beta, use the expected shortage per cycle: beta = 1 - sigma_LT x G(z) / Q, where G(z) = phi(z) - z(1 - Phi(z)) is the standard normal loss function. Solve for z. See [CSL vs fill rate](csl-vs-fill-rate.md).

Periodic review needs more: see [review policies](review-policies.md). Pooling reduces it: see [risk pooling](risk-pooling-multiechelon.md).

type: concept
title: Cycle service level vs fill rate
description: Two service targets that are not the same and how they relate
---
CSL = probability of no stockout in a replenishment cycle. Fill rate = fraction of demand met from stock.

They differ: a stockout late in a cycle may miss only a few units, so fill rate is usually higher than CSL for the same policy, especially when order quantities are large. Always ask the client which one their target means.

type: metric
title: Forecast accuracy metrics
description: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, WMAPE, MASE, bias, tracking signal, pinball loss and when to use MAPE vs WMAPE

|---|---|---|

type: method
title: Classify the demand pattern (Syntetos-Boylan)

---
The consulting answer is never "I'd use LightGBM". It is: classify the demand, set a naive baseline, pick methods per segment, validate with rolling backtests, and measure in the metric the decision uses.

|---|---|---|

title: Baselines, exponential smoothing and ARIMA
description: Naive baselines, SES/Holt/Holt-Winters, damped trend, ARIMA/SARIMA

question: What is elitism in a genetic algorithm and what size is typical?
reference: Carrying the top e individuals unchanged into the next generation so the best-so-far is never lost; a small e of 1-5% of the population N is typical.
retrieved_contexts:
---
type: concept
title: Replacement, elitism and premature convergence
description: Generational vs steady-state, elitism size, diversity fixes and monitoring
---
Replacement: generational means children replace the whole population; steady-state replaces a few worst each step.

Elitism: carry the top e individuals unchanged, so the best-so-far is never lost. Small e (1-5% of N) is typical; large e reduces diversity.

Premature convergence: the population becomes near-identical early and best fitness plateaus. Fixes: lower selection pressure (smaller tournament, see [selection](ga-selection.md)), raise mutation (or adapt it when diversity drops), fitness sharing or crowding (penalize individuals in crowded regions), island models (sub-populations with occasional migration), restarts that keep the elite.

Monitor diversity explicitly: average pairwise Hamming distance, or fitness standard deviation in the population.
---
type: concept
title: Genetic algorithm loop and encoding
description: The GA loop steps and encodings (binary, integer, real, permutation, random keys)
---
Every GA design choice controls one trade-off: selection pressure (exploit) versus diversity (explore). The probe is usually "why did you choose that operator?"

The loop:
1. Initialize a population of N candidate solutions (random, or seeded with heuristic solutions).
2. Evaluate fitness of each.
3. Select parents (biased toward fitter ones), see [selection](ga-selection.md).
4. Crossover parents to produce children (with probability pc), see [crossover and mutation](ga-crossover-mutation.md).
5. Mutate children (with small probability pm per gene).
6. Replace: form the next generation, usually keeping the best few (elitism), see [elitism and diversity](ga-elitism-diversity.md).
7. Repeat from step 2 until a stopping rule: max generations, time limit, or no improvement for k generations.

Encoding is the most important choice; it decides which operators make sense and whether children stay feasible.

| Encoding | Example problem | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Binary string | Facility open/close, knapsack | Simple; bit-flip mutation |
| Integer vector | Assign each customer to a DC | Operators must keep values in range |
| Real-valued vector | Continuous parameters, prices | Use blend or SBX crossover, Gaussian mutation |
| Permutation | TSP, job sequencing, VRP routes | Needs special crossover (OX, PMX); one-point crossover creates duplicates |
| Random keys | Any permutation problem | Real vector decoded by sorting into a permutation; any crossover stays valid |

Constraints: [GA constraint handling](ga-constraints.md).
---
type: concept
title: GA theory: schema theorem and memetic algorithms
description: What the schema theorem does and does not say, no optimality bound, memetic GA
---
Schema theorem (Holland): short, low-order, above-average schemata grow exponentially across generations. It motivates the building-block idea but is not a convergence guarantee.

No optimality guarantee and no bound: a GA cannot tell you how far you are from the optimum. That is the main argument against it when an exact method is feasible ([GA vs MILP](ga-vs-milp.md)).

Memetic algorithms: GA plus local search on each child (e.g., 2-opt). Usually much stronger than plain GA on combinatorial problems.
response: Elitism is a technique in a genetic algorithm where the top e individuals are carried unchanged to the next generation, so the best-so-far is never lost. A typical size for e is 1-5% of the population N.

title: Newsvendor model (single period)
description: Critical ratio, underage and overage cost, worked example with two salvage values
---
For perishable or seasonal items: order once, leftover is salvaged, shortage is lost.

Underage cost Cu = price - cost (margin lost per unit short). Overage cost Co = cost - salvage (loss per unit left over). F(Q*) = Cu / (Cu + Co).

Marginal argument: increase Q while the expected gain of one more unit, Cu x P(D > Q), exceeds the expected loss, Co x P(D <= Q).

Worked example: price 100, cost 60, demand ~ Normal(500, 100).
- Salvage 20: Cu = 40, Co = 40, critical ratio 0.5, so Q* = 500.

title: Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)
description: EOQ formula, robustness, worked example, EPQ and quantity discounts
---
Assumes constant known demand, fixed lead time, no shortages, instant replenishment.

Robustness: TC(Q)/TC(Q*) = 1/2 (Q/Q* + Q*/Q). Ordering 20% above Q* raises cost only about 1.7%; ordering 2x Q* raises it 25%. This flatness is why EOQ works despite rough cost inputs.

- EPQ (production rate P > demand rate D): Q* = sqrt(2DS / (h(1 - D/P))).
- Quantity discounts: compute Q* at each price; if it falls below that price's break, push it up to the break; pick the lowest total cost including purchase cost.

type: method
title: Handling constraints in a GA
description: Feasible by construction, repair, penalty, Deb's rules, death penalty
---
GA has no native way to handle constraints. Options, in rough order of preference:
1. Feasible by construction: an encoding or decoder that can only produce feasible solutions (e.g., a greedy decoder that assigns customers to the cheapest DC with remaining capacity). Best when possible.
2. Repair: fix infeasible children with a heuristic. Risk: biases the search toward the repair's habits.
3. Penalty: fitness = cost + lambda x violation. Static lambda is hard to tune; too small and the GA converges to infeasible solutions, too large and it can't cross infeasible regions to reach better feasible ones. Dynamic or adaptive lambda (raise it over generations, or when the population is mostly infeasible) helps.
4. Feasibility rules in selection (Deb's rules): feasible beats infeasible; between feasibles, lower cost wins; between infeasibles, lower violation wins. No lambda to tune.
5. Death penalty (discard infeasibles): only when feasible solutions are easy to find.

title: Replacement, elitism and premature convergence
description: Generational vs steady-state, elitism size, diversity fixes and monitoring
---
Replacement: generational means children replace the whole population; steady-state replaces a few worst each step.

Elitism: carry the top e individuals unchanged, so the best-so-far is never lost. Small e (1-5% of N) is typical; large e reduces diversity.

Premature convergence: the population becomes near-identical early and best fitness plateaus. Fixes: lower selection pressure (smaller tournament, see [selection](ga-selection.md)), raise mutation (or adapt it when diversity drops), fitness sharing or crowding (penalize individuals in crowded regions), island models (sub-populations with occasional migration), restarts that keep the elite.

Monitor diversity explicitly: average pairwise Hamming distance, or fitness standard deviation in the population.

description: The GA loop steps and encodings (binary, integer, real, permutation, random keys)
---
Every GA design choice controls one trade-off: selection pressure (exploit) versus diversity (explore). The probe is usually "why did you choose that operator?"

The loop:
1. Initialize a population of N candidate solutions (random, or seeded with heuristic solutions).
2. Evaluate fitness of each.
3. Select parents (biased toward fitter ones), see [selection](ga-selection.md).
4. Crossover parents to produce children (with probability pc), see [crossover and mutation](ga-crossover-mutation.md).
5. Mutate children (with small probability pm per gene).
6. Replace: form the next generation, usually keeping the best few (elitism), see [elitism and diversity](ga-elitism-diversity.md).
7. Repeat from step 2 until a stopping rule: max generations, time limit, or no improvement for k generations.

Encoding is the most important choice; it decides which operators make sense and whether children stay feasible.

|---|---|---|
| Binary string | Facility open/close, knapsack | Simple; bit-flip mutation |
| Integer vector | Assign each customer to a DC | Operators must keep values in range |
| Real-valued vector | Continuous parameters, prices | Use blend or SBX crossover, Gaussian mutation |
| Permutation | TSP, job sequencing, VRP routes | Needs special crossover (OX, PMX); one-point crossover creates duplicates |
| Random keys | Any permutation problem | Real vector decoded by sorting into a permutation; any crossover stays valid |

type: method
title: GA crossover and mutation operators
description: Operators per encoding, OX/PMX/CX for permutations, mutation rates
---
Crossover combines good partial solutions (building blocks) from two parents.
- Binary or integer: one-point, two-point, uniform (each gene from either parent with probability 0.5). Uniform mixes more but breaks up adjacent good genes.
- Real-valued: arithmetic (child = lambda p1 + (1 - lambda) p2), BLX-alpha (sample from an interval extended around the parents), SBX (simulated binary crossover).
- Permutation: OX (order crossover) copies a slice from parent 1 and fills the rest in the order they appear in parent 2, preserving relative order. PMX (partially mapped) copies a slice and resolves conflicts through the mapping, preserving absolute positions. CX (cycle crossover) takes each position from one parent, following cycles.
Typical pc is 0.6-0.9 in textbooks; treat it as a tuning parameter, not a rule.

Mutation keeps diversity and makes every solution reachable, so the search can escape local optima.
- Binary: flip each bit with probability about 1/L (L = string length).
- Real: add Gaussian noise; the step size can shrink over generations.
- Permutation: swap two positions, insert one element elsewhere, or invert a segment (inversion is the 2-opt move for TSP).
Too low means premature convergence; too high means random search ([diversity](ga-elitism-diversity.md)).

Operators must match the [encoding](ga-loop-and-encoding.md).

type: formula
title: Safety stock and reorder point
description: SS formulas with demand and lead-time variability, z-values, worked example and refinements
---
SS = z x sigma_d x sqrt(L) (demand variability only).
SS = z x sqrt(L x sigma_d^2 + d-bar^2 x sigma_L^2) (demand and lead-time variability).
ROP = d-bar x L + SS.

z from target cycle service level: 90% -> 1.28, 95% -> 1.645, 98% -> 2.05, 99% -> 2.33.

Worked example: d-bar = 100/day, sigma_d = 20, L = 9 days, 95% CSL.
- Demand variability only: SS = 1.645 x 20 x 3 = about 99, ROP = 900 + 99 = 999.
- Add lead-time sigma_L = 2 days: SS = 1.645 x sqrt(9 x 400 + 10,000 x 4) = 1.645 x sqrt(43,600) = about 344.

Insight to say out loud: lead-time variability more than tripled safety stock. Fixing supplier reliability can free more cash than better forecasting. Lead-time variance enters multiplied by d-bar^2, so it often dominates.

Two refinements interviewers like:
1. sigma_d should be the forecast error standard deviation, not raw demand sigma. Seasonal demand has high sigma but may be well forecast. Safety stock covers what you can't predict. Better forecasts translate directly into lower stock (see [forecast accuracy metrics](forecast-accuracy-metrics.md)); quantify that for the client in rupees, not WMAPE points.
2. The formula targets CSL. For a fill rate target beta, use the expected shortage per cycle: beta = 1 - sigma_LT x G(z) / Q, where G(z) = phi(z) - z(1 - Phi(z)) is the standard normal loss function. Solve for z. See [CSL vs fill rate](csl-vs-fill-rate.md).
